title: RIDDOR Reporting Procedure
summary: How we identify, decide on, report and record work-related deaths, injuries, occupational diseases and dangerous occurrences under RIDDOR 2013: what staff tell the office, who decides, the tests and exemptions applied in people's homes, legal and internal timescales, how reports are made and amended, who else is told, and the records kept. For all staff, with the detail for managers.

keyPoints.intro: Some accidents and illnesses connected with our work must by law be reported to the Health and Safety Executive. The Registered Manager decides and reports; your part is to tell us quickly and fully so we can meet the deadlines.
points: Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, before you leave the home about every accident, injury, near miss or equipment failure, including your own injury, and record it in the incident log before your shift ends.

Tell the office at once if anyone, including the person we support or a visitor, is taken to hospital after an accident during or connected with our visit, and tell us later what treatment they had if you find out.

If a hoist, stand aid, bath lift or stairlift collapses, overturns or a load-bearing part breaks, make the person safe, tag it DO NOT USE, leave it unrepaired where it is, and ask the person and anyone present not to use or move it.

After a death or serious injury, call 999, do only what is needed for safety, care and dignity, and leave the scene and any equipment as they are until the Registered Manager, Deputy Manager, On-call Manager or police say otherwise.

If an injury at work stops you doing your normal duties, including being moved to lighter duties, tell the HR Manager (the office if HR is closed) the same day, and again when you are back to full duties. We must count every day.
If a doctor tells you in writing that a condition is caused by your work, such as dermatitis or an infection after a needlestick injury, give a copy to the HR Manager within 2 working days.
Never decide for yourself that something does not need reporting, and never discourage anyone from reporting. A RIDDOR report is not an admission of blame, and nobody is penalised for reporting.
Agency workers tell both the office and their agency about any injury at work.

If an inspector from the Health and Safety Executive, the local authority or the Care Quality Commission contacts you about an incident, co-operate and tell the Registered Manager the same day. We give you support and paid time.

blocks.p: {{organisation}} reports every work-related death, injury, occupational disease and dangerous occurrence that the Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013 (RIDDOR) require, within the legal timescales, and keeps the records the law requires. Failing to report is a criminal offence. Making a report is not an admission of liability, and reports let the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) or the local authority decide whether to investigate.

Our staff work in people's homes, where many events look like accidents at work but are not reportable, while some that seem minor are. {{organisation}} therefore has a trained manager decide every case against the same written questions, records the reasons whether or not a report is made, and reports wherever real doubt remains. RIDDOR is separate from CQC notification, safeguarding and the duty of candour; one event may need all of them.

This procedure makes sure that every possibly reportable event reaches a trained manager quickly with the facts, is decided consistently with recorded reasons, is reported, amended and recorded on time, and that everyone who must know is told.

This procedure applies to all employees and bank workers, students on placement and agency workers, and to events affecting the people we support, their families, visitors and contractors where our work is involved. It applies wherever our work happens, including people's homes, the road and our branch offices.

It covers only RIDDOR. How every incident is recorded, investigated and learned from belongs to the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy; falls by the people we support to the Falls Prevention and Response Procedure; CQC notifications to the Statutory Notifications to CQC Procedure; first aid and emergency department attendance after a needlestick, bite or splash to the Sharps Safety and Needlestick Injury Procedure; equipment failure and the hoist and sling register to the Hoists, Slings and Lifting Equipment Procedure; and abuse or neglect to the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure.

rows: Accident

A separate, identifiable and unintended event that causes physical injury. It includes non-consensual physical violence to a person at work. Gradual harm, such as back pain from months of repetitive handling, is not an accident.
Work-related

Arising out of or in connection with work: the way the work was organised, carried out or supervised, the equipment or substances used, or the condition of the place of work contributed. Nobody needs to be at fault.
Worker

Our employees and bank workers, and students on placement with us, whom the Health and Safety (Training for Employment) Regulations 1990 treat as our employees. A person not at work means the people we support, their families, visitors and the public.
Specified injury

To a worker: a fracture other than to a finger, thumb or toe; an amputation; an injury likely to cause permanent loss or reduction of sight; a crush injury to the head or torso damaging the brain or internal organs; a burn or scald covering more than 10% of the body or damaging the eyes, breathing or other vital organs; scalping needing hospital treatment; loss of consciousness from a head injury or asphyxia; an enclosed-space injury causing hypothermia or heat illness or needing resuscitation or more than 24 hours in hospital.
Over-seven-day injury

An accident leaves a worker unable to do their normal work for more than 7 consecutive days, not counting the day of the accident but counting weekends, days the worker was not rostered and days on lighter duties, such as visits with no moving and handling. More than 3 such days is an over-three-day injury, which is recorded but not reported.
Hospital treatment
Treatment at a hospital for a person taken there directly from the scene by any means. Examinations, X-rays and other diagnostic tests alone are not treatment.
Dangerous occurrence
A near-miss event listed in Schedule 2 to RIDDOR that could have caused serious harm, whether or not anyone was hurt.
Responsible person

The person who must report: us as employer for our workers wherever they work and, under HSE guidance for domestic premises, us as the employer in control of the work activity when a person not at work is injured, or a dangerous occurrence happens, in a home in connection with our work.

blocks.p: The Directors are told within 24 hours of every reportable event and challenge the quarterly figures. The Nominated Individual decides and reports only when the Registered Manager and Deputy Manager are both unavailable, notifies our insurers and leads on any enforcement action against {{organisation}}.

As Health and Safety Lead, the Registered Manager acts for {{organisation}} as responsible person: screens events, decides, makes and amends reports, records every decision with reasons, tells the others listed in this procedure and is the single point of contact for inspectors. The Deputy Manager covers all of these duties in the Registered Manager's absence and carries out the checks in the Monitoring and review section.

Out of hours the On-call Manager never makes a RIDDOR decision. They phone the escalation manager (the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager on the management escalation rota) at once about any event in the immediate escalation table, make sure the incident log entry is complete, and hand over everything else by 10am on the next working day.

The HR Manager counts the days a worker cannot do normal work after a work-related accident, checks every fit note and occupational health report for a diagnosis linking a condition to work, obtains agencies' written confirmations, and tells the Registered Manager the same working day when a trigger in this procedure is reached.

subsections.heading: Care Coordinators, Field Care Supervisors and Office staff

blocks.p: Office staff escalate events as the Reporting events to the office section sets out. When facts are missing, such as whether a person received hospital treatment, the Care Coordinator or Field Care Supervisor obtains them within 1 working day from the worker, the person or, with the person's agreement, their family, and adds them to the incident log entry.

Nobody is discouraged from reporting or penalised for it. Every member of staff follows these steps after any accident, injury, near miss, equipment failure or dangerous event connected with our work:

steps: Make the situation safe, give first aid within your training and call 999 if anyone needs emergency help, staying with them as the First Aid Procedure sets out.

After a death or serious injury, do only what is needed for safety, care and dignity, and leave the scene and any equipment as they are until the Registered Manager, Deputy Manager, On-call Manager or police say otherwise.

If lifting or other care equipment has failed, tie on a DO NOT USE tag from your kit box and tell the person and anyone present why. Do not repair, move or throw away any part of it, and ask them not to, as the Hoists, Slings and Lifting Equipment Procedure requires.

Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, before you leave the home or scene and speak to a person. If nobody answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly.

Record the event in the incident log before the end of your shift: who was involved, what happened in order, when and where, the injury and its body location, any equipment (make, model and serial number from the label), witnesses, whether anyone went to hospital and how, and what was done.

Tell the office about anything you learn later, such as hospital treatment or a change in the injured person's condition. If your own injury stops you doing your normal duties, tell the HR Manager (the office if HR is closed) the same day and again when you return to full duties, and give the HR Manager a copy of any written diagnosis linking a condition to your work within 2 working days. Agency workers also tell their agency.

blocks.p: Office staff, or the On-call Manager out of hours, pass these events to the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager (the escalation manager out of hours) at once, by phone:

rows: Any death that may be connected with our work
A person dies after a fall from a hoist.
A worker's injury that may be a specified injury
Suspected fracture other than a finger, thumb or toe; serious burn or scald; head injury with any loss of consciousness; eye injury.
Anyone not at work taken to hospital after an accident during or connected with our work
A person scalded in a bath we were giving; a relative trips over our equipment.
Possible dangerous occurrence

A hoist, stand aid, bath lift or stairlift collapses, overturns or a load-bearing part fails; an electrical fire in equipment our staff were using; a fire our work may have caused; a sharps injury, bite, scratch or splash from a source known to carry hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV.

sections.heading: Deciding whether an event is reportable

blocks.p: The Registered Manager screens every incident log entry that records an injury, ill health, a hospital attendance, an equipment failure, an exposure to blood or body fluids, a fire or an electrical incident, and every report from the HR Manager. A death that may be work-related is decided at once, at any hour, by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager. Any other event in the immediate escalation table is decided the same working day it reaches the office, or by 12 noon on the next working day if reported out of hours; every other event at its initial review under the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy, and a report from the HR Manager by the end of the next working day. The questions, in order, are:

steps: Was there an accident, a dangerous occurrence or a reportable diagnosis?
Was it work-related, applying the tests below?
Does the outcome meet a threshold in the table in the Making the report section?

blocks.p: The decision is recorded in the management notes of the incident log entry's review as reportable, not reportable or pending, with the reasons and the guidance relied on. A pending decision names the fact awaited, who is obtaining it and the date by which it will be decided. The work-related test is applied honestly: a report is never avoided to protect our record or a member of staff.

subsections.heading: Injuries to the people we support and other people not at work

blocks.p: An injury to a person not at work is reportable when it results from a work-related accident and the person is taken directly from the scene to hospital for treatment; their death from such an accident is always reportable. Following HSE's health and social care guidance, the Registered Manager checks the care plan and risk assessments to see what care was assessed as needed and whether it was given.

rows: The person is scalded by bath water during care, or slides through or falls from a sling or hoist, for example because the wrong sling size was used.
The person falls when alone, the care plan assessed no need for supervision or equipment, and nothing about our equipment, methods or the home contributed.
The person falls during a transfer our staff were assisting, or because care the plan required, such as help to the toilet, was not given.
The person is found on the floor with no work-related factor, or chose to get up without the help the care plan offered.
The person's limb is trapped in bed rails our staff raised, or someone trips over our equipment or a hazard our staff created.
Self-harm or suicide, which are not accidents; or an assault on the person by someone not at work.
A relative or visitor is injured by equipment our staff were using.

Injury arising from medical treatment laid down by a doctor or dentist, such as a reaction to a medicine given as prescribed (the medical treatment exemption). Medicines errors are decided with the external adviser.

blocks.p: A slip on an icy path at a person's home, a back injury while helping a person to stand or a scald during a visit is reportable if it causes a specified injury or an over-seven-day injury. Physical violence to a worker by a person we support, a relative or a member of the public is an accident on the same thresholds, as the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy explains. Verbal abuse and threats without physical injury are not reportable, nor is an injury from a dispute between colleagues about a personal matter.

Injuries caused by a vehicle moving on a road, such as a collision while driving between visits, are not reportable and are handled under the Driving at Work Policy. They remain reportable where the worker was loading or unloading a vehicle, such as lifting a wheelchair into a car boot, or was hurt by someone who was.

The count starts the day after the accident. After an accident on a Monday, if the worker still cannot do full normal work on the Tuesday of the following week, the eighth day, the injury is reportable within 15 days of the accident. The HR Manager checks the worker's status on the fourth and eighth days (the next working day if either falls on a non-working day) and tells the Registered Manager the same working day.

The collapse, overturning or failure of any load-bearing part of a hoist, stand aid, bath lift, stairlift or other lifting equipment is a dangerous occurrence under Schedule 2 paragraph 1, whether or not anyone is hurt. Failure of a sling alone is not, because slings are accessories for lifting, although an injury it causes may be reportable. We report a dangerous occurrence that happens in a person's home in connection with our work, such as a hoist our staff were operating. A failure while family or another provider use the equipment without our staff is not ours to report; staff who find it tag it and phone the office, and the Care Coordinator tells the owner and that provider the same working day.

We also report an electrical short circuit or overload causing a fire or explosion in equipment our staff were using, where it causes a significant risk of death or puts the equipment out of use for more than 24 hours (paragraph 4); an unintentional fire or explosion connected with our work that stops normal work in a branch office, or our visits to a person's home, for more than 24 hours (paragraph 25); and, as the Sharps Safety and Needlestick Injury Procedure sets out under paragraph 10, a sharps injury from a source known to carry hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV and, as our policy, a bite, scratch or splash from such a source or a sharps injury whose source is later found to carry one of these viruses.

A disease is reportable only when a registered medical practitioner diagnoses it in writing and the worker's job involves the linked work. For care work these are occupational dermatitis (significant or regular exposure to a known skin irritant or sensitiser, such as wet work or glove chemicals), occupational asthma (exposure to a known respiratory sensitiser), cramp of the hand or forearm (prolonged repetitive movement), tendonitis or tenosynovitis of the hand or forearm (physically demanding, frequently repetitive work), and any disease attributed to a biological agent at work, such as tuberculosis, hepatitis B or C or HIV caught from a person we support, including an infection without symptoms. An infection as likely to come from the community, such as flu or COVID-19, is reportable only where work was more likely than not the source. Colonisation, such as with MRSA, and stress are not reportable.

A diagnosis or fit note from a nurse, physiotherapist or other non-doctor does not trigger a report. HSE consulted in 2026 on widening who may diagnose and on adding diseases and dangerous occurrences; no change is in force, and we apply RIDDOR 2013 as it stands.

The Registered Manager checks HSE's information sheet HSIS1 and HSE's RIDDOR guidance pages first. If doubt remains, they ask our external health and safety adviser the same working day. If doubt still remains, we report. Where facts needed for a 10-day deadline are still missing 5 working days after the event, we report on the information we have and amend the report when the facts are known.

blocks.p: A complete online report made without delay meets both the duty to notify and the duty to report within 10 days.

steps: Use HSE's online RIDDOR forms: report of an injury (which covers deaths), of a dangerous occurrence or of a case of disease.

For a death or a specified injury to a worker, the Registered Manager may instead phone HSE's Incident Contact Centre, which takes only these reports, on weekdays from 8.30am to 5pm. After a work-related death outside those hours, the deciding manager also phones HSE's out-of-hours duty officer at once. The numbers are kept in the branch health and safety file.

Code the incident as HSE directs for care in people's own homes: main industry Government administrative functions, Education, Health; activity Non-residential social work, Elderly, disabled. Use this code whoever was injured, and never Accommodation.
Give the facts plainly, without opinion or blame. For a blood-borne virus infection the worker need not be named, as HSE allows.
Add HSE to the incident log entry's external bodies with the RIDDOR reference and date, attach the downloaded copy of the submitted form, and note the time, method and who reported.

blocks.p: When new facts change a report, including an investigation finding, a different diagnosis or a later death, the Registered Manager submits a duplicate online form within 2 working days of learning the facts (within 1 working day for a death), resubmitting all the information and starting the description with the words Amendment to Incident Reference Number followed by the reference. Changes to a fatal or specified injury report may instead be phoned to the Incident Contact Centre.

An agency is normally the legal employer of its workers and reports their injuries. The Registered Manager tells the agency about any injury to its worker the same working day with the facts it needs, and the HR Manager obtains the agency's written confirmation of its decision and any RIDDOR reference within 5 working days and attaches it to the incident log entry. Where the agency confirms that the worker is self-employed, or gives no confirmation by then, the Registered Manager makes any report needed. Our agency agreements state these arrangements. We report injuries to students on placement as injuries to our employees and tell their college the same working day.
A RIDDOR report reaches only HSE or the local authority. The Registered Manager makes sure these are also told:

blocks.p: When an inspector from HSE, the local authority or CQC contacts anyone about an incident, the Registered Manager is told and tells the Nominated Individual (at once for an enforcement notice) and the Directors the same day. The Registered Manager supplies documents by the inspector's deadline and logs what was supplied. An enforcement notice also goes to the Directors within 24 hours and onto the risk register under the Risk Management Policy. Staff asked for an interview have paid time and may be accompanied by a colleague or representative; for an interview under caution, the Nominated Individual arranges legal advice for {{organisation}} and tells the worker they may take their own.

Every reportable event is investigated under the Incident Reporting, Investigation and Learning Policy. For a death, a specified injury or a dangerous occurrence, the Registered Manager involves our external health and safety adviser in the investigation. Equipment involved stays out of use until the Registered Manager agrees.

A reportable event found to have been missed or reported late is reported at once, the delay is recorded in the incident log, the Nominated Individual is told within 1 working day and the cause is added to the service improvement plan.

blocks.p: Any wrong or late decision becomes an action in the service improvement plan with an owner and deadline. This procedure is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager, consulting the representatives of employee safety, and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy. It is reviewed sooner after a change in law or HSE guidance, including any change arising from HSE's 2026 RIDDOR consultation, a late or missed report, an enforcement action or inspection finding, or when monitoring shows the arrangements are not working.
